findings.body: Normalizing a database identifier with `PurePath(...).name` creates a dangerous mismatch between the ID provided by the client and the ID queried in the database. An attacker can craft an ID containing path separators that bypasses validation or authorization checks but resolves to a victim's ID in the query. Furthermore, `PurePath` behavior depends on the host operating system (treating `\` as a separator only on Windows), leading to inconsistent security boundaries across environments. Identifiers should be queried exactly as provided or strictly validated, not silently truncated.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies an ID like `attacker/../admin`. An authorization layer approves the request based on the `attacker` prefix, but `PurePath` extracts `admin`, causing the query to return the admin's record and granting unauthorized access.
findings.title: Unsafe identifier normalization enables authorization bypass

findings.body: Because `canonicalize()` fails if a path does not exist, an attacker can use this function as a filesystem oracle. If they supply an absolute path or use `../` to point outside `root`, `canonicalize()` will return `NotFound` if the file does not exist, but will succeed if it does exist (whereupon `strip_prefix` will catch it and return `PermissionDenied`). This allows an attacker to scan the host filesystem to determine exactly which files and directories exist. To eliminate this information leak, map both `canonicalize` and `strip_prefix` errors to `NotFound` so that unauthorized paths are indistinguishable from non-existent ones.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker requests a report named `../../../../etc/shadow`. If the file exists, `canonicalize` succeeds and `strip_prefix` returns `PermissionDenied`. findings.anchor: var statement = db.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
findings.body: Returning a `ResultSet` leaves the underlying `PreparedStatement` open. Because the caller only receives the `ResultSet`, the statement is never closed, leading to a resource leak. Calling `closeOnCompletion()` ensures the statement is closed automatically when the caller closes the `ResultSet`.
findings.failure_scenario: Each call to `find` leaks a `PreparedStatement`. Over time, this exhausts the database's open cursor limit (e.g., `ORA-01000`), causing subsequent queries to fail.
findings.suggestion:
var statement = db.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
    statement.closeOnCompletion();
findings.title: Call closeOnCompletion() to prevent statement leaks

findings.title: Avoid deprecated, timezone-naive datetime.utcnow()

findings.body: Extracting the filename component of `user_id` using `PurePath` truncates any input containing slashes. If the application performs authorization checks on the full `user_id` before this function is called, an attacker can bypass those checks by appending a slash and a target user's ID (e.g., `authorized_user/target_user`). The authorization check will see the safe prefix, but the database query will execute against `target_user`. Remove this normalization and query the database using the exact `user_id` provided.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker provides `user_id` as `my_id/admin`. An upstream authorization check validates that the ID starts with `my_id`, but `PurePath(...).name` truncates it to `admin`. The query returns the admin user's data, resulting in an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) or privilege escalation.
findings.title: Unsafe truncation of database identifier

findings.body: Validating a path using `canonicalize` followed by `File::open` introduces a Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) race condition. If an attacker has write access to the directory, they can swap a validated directory with a symlink to a sensitive location after `canonicalize` succeeds but before `File::open` is called. `File::open` will then follow the symlink outside the intended root. To fix this securely, use a directory-based API like the `cap-std` crate (`Dir::open`), or use OS-specific flags like `O_NOFOLLOW` combined with manual component-by-component resolution.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker creates a directory and a file (e.g., `dir/passwd`), which passes the `canonicalize` and `strip_prefix` checks. Before `File::open` executes, the attacker replaces `dir` with a symlink to `/etc`. `File::open` follows the symlink, opening `/etc/passwd` and bypassing the directory restriction.
findings.title: Path validation is vulnerable to a TOCTOU race condition

ground_truth.clean_trap: An untrusted name is joined to a root, but both paths are canonicalized and strip_prefix enforces containment before opening.

findings.body: Extracting the filename component of `user_id` using `PurePath` truncates any input containing slashes. If the application performs authorization checks on the full `user_id` before this function is called, an attacker can bypass those checks by appending a slash and a target user's ID (e.g., `authorized_user/target_user`). The authorization check will see the safe prefix, but the database query will execute against `target_user`. Remove this normalization and query the database using the exact `user_id` provided.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker provides `user_id` as `my_id/admin`. An upstream authorization check validates that the ID starts with `my_id`, but `PurePath(...).name` truncates it to `admin`. The query returns the admin user's data, resulting in an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) or privilege escalation.
findings.title: Unsafe truncation of database identifier

findings.body: The assertion was changed from an exact array match (`toEqual`) to a loose boolean check (`toBeTruthy`). This hides the fact that `renderReport` now drops the first row, as any array (even an empty one) is truthy in JavaScript.

findings.body: Interpolating `userName` directly into a shell command string allows arbitrary command execution if the username contains shell metacharacters. Revert to using `spawnSync` (which requires updating the import) or `execFileSync` with an argument array to safely pass user input.
findings.failure_scenario: If `userName` is `"alice; rm -rf /"`, the shell executes `report --user alice` followed by `rm -rf /`, leading to arbitrary command execution and potential system compromise.

findings.body: Validating a path using `canonicalize` followed by `File::open` introduces a Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) race condition. If an attacker has write access to the directory, they can swap a validated directory with a symlink to a sensitive location after `canonicalize` succeeds but before `File::open` is called. `File::open` will then follow the symlink outside the intended root. To fix this securely, use a directory-based API like the `cap-std` crate (`Dir::open`), or use OS-specific flags like `O_NOFOLLOW` combined with manual component-by-component resolution.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker creates a directory and a file (e.g., `dir/passwd`), which passes the `canonicalize` and `strip_prefix` checks. Before `File::open` executes, the attacker replaces `dir` with a symlink to `/etc`. `File::open` follows the symlink, opening `/etc/passwd` and bypassing the directory restriction.
findings.title: Path validation is vulnerable to a TOCTOU race condition

ground_truth.clean_trap: An untrusted name is joined to a root, but both paths are canonicalized and strip_prefix enforces containment before opening.

findings.failure_scenario: Deprecated methods represent technical debt and may be removed in future Java releases. Furthermore, `Date` lacks robust timezone handling, which can lead to formatting bugs.
